newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian oil workers threaten to shut down sector.
newsitem.headline: Colombian oil workers threaten to shut down sector.

text.p: Colombia's main oil workers' union is preparing to "shut down" the state-run oil sector in the face of the government's refusal to cede on labor demands, union leader Hernando Hernandez said Sunday.
He declined to say exactly when the 7,000-strong USO union may move to paralyze the refining, production and pumping operations of the state-run oil compant Ecopetrol, citing security reasons.

"We are working internally (in the union) for this action which will paralyze production, refining and all other activities because we see the governmment has no real will to negotiate," Hernndez said.

If the USO suceeds in plans to shut down the state oil industry it would mean more than 400,000 barrels per day in lost production and a halt to the average daily throughput of 260,000 barrels in the two main state-owned refiniries in Barrancabermeja and Cartagena.

Mines and Energy Minister Rodrigo Villamizar said Colombia had enough fuel supplies to last almost three weeks and that any shortfalls would be offset by increasing imports. Hernndez, however, claimed that fuel supplies would last just eight days.

The USO union is already taking a lead role in the nationwide, state workers strike, now in its sixth day but until now it has allowed non-unionized Ecopetrol employees to run operations as part of the company's contigency plans.
The USO's threats to step up strike action come the day before the expiry of a deadline for an agreement between the union and the government on a new collective contract.

USO, known for its combative and fiercely nationalistic stance, is calling for a 30 percent pay hike for its members and an end to what it claims are plans for the creeping privatization of Ecopetrol. It has also protested vociferously at the arrest of scores of its members on charges of links with the National Liberation Army (ELN), Colombia's second largest guerrilla force, which specializes in attacks on oil infrastructure and multinational companies.

Many of the USO demands have been included in the basic list of proposals being put forward by a joint command of unions heading the strike by an estimated 800,000 public sector workers, which began at midnight last Monday.

The planned escalation in the USO's industrial action could feasibly affect private sector, multinational oil companies if it halts pumping activities. A 24-hour stoppage in October paralyzed the country's two main oil pipelines, which together pump more than 300,000 barrels per day.
The government seems likely to outlaw USO efforts to paralyze the sector, arguing that the oil industry is an essential service.
